title: Add 1 to a very big number
hook: Rounding errors hide in far decimal places. Surely whole numbers are safe?

knows: that 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 on a computer (pennies-dont-add-up)
doesNotKnow: that big numbers lose whole integers, not just tiny fractions
that a JavaScript number has 53 bits of precision

misconception: Rounding errors only hide in far decimal places; whole numbers are always safe.
objective: The learner can explain that a JavaScript number (a double) holds every whole number only up to 2^53 = 9007199254740992; beyond it only every second whole number exists, so 9007199254740992 + 1 is rounded back to 9007199254740992 while + 2 works.

claims.text: In JavaScript, 9007199254740992 + 1 comes out as 9007199254740992, with no error or warning.
claims.source: Builder ran in Node 22: 2**53 + 1 === 2**53 is true. The stage computes the sums with real JavaScript arithmetic (Demo.tsx add()), and option B is the string of P + 1.

claims.text: A JavaScript number is a double (IEEE 754 binary64) with 53 bits of precision.
claims.source: ECMAScript 2024 Language Specification, 6.1.6.1 The Number Type (IEEE 754-2019 binary64); IEEE 754 binary64 has a 53-bit significand (52 stored + 1 implicit).

claims.text: Every whole number up to 2^53 = 9007199254740992 fits exactly, but beyond it only every second whole number exists; Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER is 2^53 − 1.
claims.source: ECMAScript 2024, 21.1.2.6 Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 - 1); spacing of binary64 values in [2^53, 2^54) is 2. Builder checked: Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER === 2**53 - 1; the stage's dots come from a BigInt round trip (Demo.tsx exact()). · DISPUTED 2026-10-13 (pass 3): Wording overreach: "beyond it only every second whole number exists" is true only up to 2^54; from 2^54 up only every fourth number exists, and so on. Immediately above 2^53 (all the stage shows) it is exact. Fix: "just beyond it (up to 2^54) only every second whole number exists", or "beyond it, whole numbers start to be skipped, first every second one". Rest of the claim (exact up to 2^53; MAX_SAFE_INTEGER = 2^53 - 1) verified.

claims.text: Past 2^53, adding 1 lands exactly halfway between two numbers and is rounded to the even one, so it either does nothing or jumps by 2; adding 2 moves 9007199254740992 to 9007199254740994.
claims.source: Round-half-to-even is IEEE 754's default rounding (roundTiesToEven, 4.3.1). Builder ran in Node: 2**53 + 2 = 9007199254740994; (2**53 + 2) + 1 = 9007199254740996; (2**53 + 4) + 1 = 9007199254740996.

claims.text: For exact big integers, JavaScript has BigInt.

recall.question: A JavaScript program stores order IDs as ordinary numbers. Around 9,007,199,254,740,993 two different IDs start comparing as equal. Why?
options: The IDs overflowed and became negative
Past 2^53 a JavaScript number cannot hold every whole number, so neighbours round to the same value
recall.why: A double has 53 bits of precision, so beyond 2^53 only every second whole number exists and an odd ID is rounded onto its neighbour.
